families.s: HSE control of natural-rubber-latex allergy in health and social care
families.t: latex proteins, gloves, asthma, dermatitis, anaphylaxis, substitution, glove selection, exposure assessment and occupational health
f: Natural rubber latex contains proteins capable of causing allergy.
Latex is used in medical gloves and a range of healthcare devices.
Latex proteins can cause occupational asthma and dermatitis.
Severe allergic reactions including anaphylaxis are possible although uncommon.
Employers should assess direct and indirect exposure to workers and other people.
Glove selection should consider whether latex is necessary and whether a safer alternative is suitable.
High-protein and powdered latex gloves can increase airborne and skin exposure.
Most affected workers can be managed with effective controls and occupational-health input rather than automatic removal from work.
families.g: Latex-allergy risk depends on product protein and powder, glove use frequency, airborne and skin exposure, sensitisation, substitution, infection-control needs, worker symptoms and occupational-health management.

families.s: HSE management, classification and transport of healthcare waste
families.t: infection, classification, segregation, storage, transport, infectious waste, dangerous goods, ambulance, dental, community and compliance
f: Effective healthcare-waste management is necessary to prevent infection and other health and safety risks.
Providers must consider infection-control and health and safety legislation.
Environmental, waste and transport legislation may also apply.
Waste types should be correctly classified.
Waste should be segregated and stored safely according to its classification.
Transport arrangements should reflect the hazards and applicable dangerous-goods controls.
Bloodborne-virus contaminated waste should be treated as hazardous unless effectively inactivated.
Healthcare-waste arrangements apply across hospitals, ambulances, laboratories, pharmacies, GP practices, health centres and dental practices.
families.g: Healthcare-waste risk depends on waste type and infection status, sharps and drugs, segregation and packaging, storage, handling, transport, community setting, training and legal classification.

families.s: HSE RIDDOR reporting and coding for health and social care
families.t: employees, service users, work relationship, specified injuries, diseases, dangerous occurrences, coding, records and investigation
f: HSE provides sector-specific guidance for deciding whether health and social care incidents are RIDDOR-reportable.
Reportability depends on the event, who was affected and the relationship to work activity.
Specified employee injuries may be reportable.
Certain diagnosed occupational diseases may be reportable.
Specified dangerous occurrences can be reportable even without injury.
Incidents involving service users are not automatically reportable merely because harm occurred.
Reports should be coded correctly in HSE's online system.
Internal records and investigation remain important even when an event is not reportable.
families.g: RIDDOR duty depends on person affected, employment status, event and outcome, work relationship, diagnosis, timing, statutory category, regulator and the evidence from investigation.

families.s: HSE slips, trips and same-level falls control in health and social care
families.t: cleaning, body fluids, dust, flooring, footwear, lighting, contrast, obstructions, stairs and human factors
f: Slips, trips and falls can seriously affect both employees and people receiving care.
They account for around half of reported major injuries to employees in the sector.
Assessments should consider everyone with access and the physical and environmental factors that create falls.
Water, cleaning residues, body fluids, dust, lint and talcum powder can contaminate floors.
Slip-resistant flooring may be expected in regularly contaminated areas such as kitchens, bathrooms and entrances.
Trolleys, cables, stored items, uneven surfaces and changes of level can create trip hazards.
Handrails, lighting and visual contrast can help vulnerable people navigate safely.
Stairs should be maintained, suitable for their use and considered in individual care plans.
families.g: Care-sector slip and fall risk depends on floor and contamination, cleaning and drying, footwear, lighting and contrast, mobility, obstacles, stairs, work organisation and maintenance.

families.s: HSE prevention and management of violence and aggression in health and social care
families.t: abuse, threats, assault, under-reporting, risk assessment, care needs, staffing, training, reporting, learning and worker support
f: Health and social care staff should not accept violent or aggressive behaviour as a normal part of the job.
Work-related violence includes abuse, threats and assault connected with work.
Violence and aggression are a major source of reportable injuries in the sector.
Under-reporting is common because some staff regard incidents as part of the job.
Employers should gather information from incidents, workers and relevant agencies to assess risks.
Controls should reflect service-user needs, staffing, environment, communication and foreseeable triggers.
Staff need information, instruction and training appropriate to the risk.
Incidents should be reported, investigated and used to improve controls and worker support.
families.g: Violence risk depends on service and client needs, environment, lone work, staffing and waiting, communication, history and triggers, training, reporting culture and post-incident support.
